description: We are TEAM UMAIR, a creative team participating in the Faisalabad Local Event. We're tackling "The Earth Information Jukebox" turning NASA Earth data and imagery into sound for a multisensory experience. We're looking for teammates with skills in coding, web development, data visualization, or multimedia/audio design. If you love space, sound, and creative tech, join us!
summary: Hear the Air turns NASA's GEOS Aerosols visualization into an interactive listening experience. Wildfire smoke, desert dust, sea salt and sulfates are invisible to most of us, and NASA's aerosol model shows them only as colour. We analysed NASA SVS 5572 (August–September 2024) frame by frame with OpenCV, measured how much of each frame every colour family covers, and turned those measurements into four distinct, synchronised voices that play live in the browser: a low pulse for smoke, gusts of wind for dust, plucked notes for sea salt and bells for sulfates. Visitors watch the model wrapped around a 3D Earth, hear the atmosphere move, solo any aerosol, jump to its peak moment and read a plain-language description of what they are hearing. The project answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by giving Earth science a second doorway — sound — that works for blind and low-vision audiences as well as anyone curious. It is a historical model sonification, not a live air-quality or health service.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Hear the Air lets people listen to Earth's atmosphere. It plays NASA's GEOS Aerosols visualization (SVS 5572) wrapped around an interactive 3D globe and, in sync, generates four sound voices — one for each aerosol family NASA colours in the model:

• Wildfire smoke (orange/red) → a low pulse that beats faster as smoke coverage rises

• Dust (magenta) → gusts of wind that sweep more often and brighter as dust grows

• Sea salt (blue) → plucked notes that move faster and climb higher

• Sulfates (green) → shimmering bells that ring more often

All four play in D major pentatonic over a soft pad, so they always sound musical together.

HOW IT WORKS

1. NASA source: GEOS Aerosols animation, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS 5572, 1 Aug – 14 Sep 2024).

2. Offline analysis (Python, OpenCV, NumPy): one frame per second is sampled, the legend and labels are cropped out, and each frame is converted to HSV to measure the share of pixels in each NASA colour family.

3. Timeline: 74 timestamped samples stored in a 10 KB JSON file — no server, no database.

4. Browser audio (Web Audio API): the current sample drives each voice. Each voice follows its own range across the 45 days so quiet layers like smoke stay audible. Reverb, echo, a compressor and a limiter keep the sound rich but gentle.

5. Visuals (Next.js, React, three.js): the same NASA video is mapped live onto a 3D Earth with an atmosphere glow and orbiting particles that pulse with each voice, plus a live spectrum scope, a four-line "signal river" of the full dataset, and a live text description.

FEATURES

Play/pause, seek, replay; solo or mute any voice; per-voice intensity and master volume; presets and a story mode that jumps between peaks; compare two moments; jump to each aerosol's peak; audio-only view; keyboard shortcuts (Space, 1–4, M, A, R); live plain-language description for screen readers; reduced-motion support.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Earth science is usually shown visually, which excludes blind and low-vision audiences and makes dense models hard for everyone. Hear the Air gives a second, auditory way to notice patterns — the Saharan dust plume crossing the Atlantic, smoke over the Amazon and Africa — and makes the science more memorable.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, three.js (WebGL), Web Audio API, Python, OpenCV, NumPy, FFmpeg, Vercel.

CREATIVITY

Every sound is driven by measurements of NASA's own frames, and the NASA visualization itself becomes the surface of a 3D Earth that reacts to its own sound.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (relative visual coverage in a historical model — not concentrations, PM2.5 or health risk, and the site says so); accessibility (keyboard control, screen-reader descriptions, audio-only mode, capped volume, reduced motion); performance (no backend, lazy-loaded 3D, compressed video); originality (our own data pipeline, sound design and interface)
